title: Scalable information extraction from free text electronic health records using large language models
abstract: ABSTRACT Background A vast amount of potentially useful information such as description of patient symptoms, family, and social history is recorded as free-text notes in electronic health records (EHRs) but is difficult to reliably extract at scale, limiting their utility in research. This study aims to assess whether an “out of the box” implementation of open-source large language models (LLMs) without any fine-tuning can accurately extract social determinants of health (SDoH) data from free-text clinical notes. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study using EHR data from the Mass General Brigham (MGB) system, analyzing free-text notes for SDoH information. We selected a random sample of 200 patients and manually labeled nine SDoH aspects. Eight advanced open-source LLMs were evaluated against a baseline pattern-matching model. Two human reviewers provided the manual labels, achieving 93% inter-annotator agreement. LLM performance was assessed using accuracy metrics for overall, mentioned, and non-mentioned SDoH, and macro F1 scores. Results LLMs outperformed the baseline pattern-matching approach, particularly for explicitly mentioned SDoH, achieving up to 40% higher Accuracy mentioned . openchat_3.5 was the best-performing model, surpassing the baseline in overall accuracy across all nine SDoH aspects. The refined pipeline with prompt engineering reduced hallucinations and improved accuracy. Conclusions Open-source LLMs are effective and scalable tools for extracting SDoH from unstructured EHRs, surpassing traditional pattern-matching methods. Further refinement and domain-specific training could enhance their utility in clinical research and predictive analytics, improving healthcare outcomes and addressing health disparities.

claims.text: The pattern-matching baseline model achieved a 77.33% average overall accuracy across nine SDoH aspects.
openchat_3.5 achieved over 40% higher average Accuracy_mentioned than the pattern-matching baseline model.
Llama-2-13b-chat was the only evaluated LLM with a significantly lower average Accuracy_mentioned compared to the baseline.
Two human reviewers achieved 93% inter-annotator agreement on manual labeling of 9 SDoH aspects across 200 patient records.
The pattern-matching baseline model achieved an average Accuracy_non-mentioned of 96.66%.
Model quantization did not substantially compromise LLM performance on SDoH extraction tasks.

limitations.text: Traditional rule-based NLP approaches are constrained by their lack of generalizability across different datasets and settings.
Machine learning-based NLP models rely heavily on the costly step of manual data annotation for model training, making them harder to scale.
The prompt engineering and LLM response postprocessing steps involve complexity and subjectivity.
Observations regarding model performance based on general SDoH concepts may not extrapolate to other, more complex clinical feature extraction tasks.
Premise prompts designed to reduce hallucination in the refined pipeline reduced sensitivity to SDoH features mentioned in the text.

future_work.text: Conduct specific training or fine-tuning of open-source LLMs on free-text EHRs for extracting more complex clinical concepts.

methodologies.name: Zero-shot open-source LLM extraction pipeline with prompt engineering
methodologies.description: A question-answering framework using eight open-source LLMs with prompt engineering, AWQ quantization, and post-processing pattern matching to extract nine SDoH categories from unstructured clinical notes.
